newsitem.title: UK: Historic Scottish crowning stone goes home.
newsitem.headline: Historic Scottish crowning stone goes home.

text.p: Scotland's historic Stone of Scone on which Scottish Kings were crowned until it was seized 700 years ago by English King Edward I took the high road home on Thursday.
The official border handover of the giant slab was to take place on a bridge crossing the river Tweed at the Scottish border town of Coldstream on Friday.
"The moment when the Stone returns to Scottish soil will be very special for all Scots," Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth said.
Military bands will lead a procession into Coldstream town centre when the stone arrives.
Coldstream is believed to be the border crossing where Edward I passed through when he took the stone to England.

Since 1296 the stone has lived under a throne in London's Westminster Abbey, where England's Kings and Queens have traditionally been crowned. It is due to be taken to Edinburgh, Scotland's capital, on Friday.
Once there experts will decide if it needs restoration work before it goes on view to the public at Edinburgh Castle on December 1.
The Duke of York is due to attend a ceremonial handover of the stone at the castle on November 30, the festival of St. Andrew, Scotland's patron saint.

It is believed the stone was first used in the coronation of a Scottish King in 839, at the village of Scone in southeast Scotland. It served as the coronation stone for all subsequent Scottish Kings until Edward I arrived to subdue Scottish rebels.

It disappeared in 1950 when it was stolen from Westminster Abbey and smuggled back to Scotland by a group of Scottish Nationalists, but was returned to its housing in Westminster when it was found four months later.
